items.title: European Central Bank sees ‘historical parallels with the dotcom and subprime bubbles’ because of AI’s ‘rapid shift’ into debt finance
items.summary:
For most of this year, markets have been asking how big the AI bubble is and how bad it gets if it pops. On Wednesday, the European Central Bank went through the boom against the last big credit bust, point by point, using the companies’ own filings.

In its twice-yearly Financial Stability Review , the ECB estimated that big tech firms had “total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than USD 4 trillion as of the second quarter of 2026,” which it said was “well in excess of their outstanding on-balance-sheet liabilities.” The sample is Alphabet , Amazon , Meta , Microsoft , Nvidia , Oracle , Broadcom and Anthropic. “The rapid shift towards debt finance invokes historical parallels with the dotcom and subprime bubbles,” the central bank wrote.

The ECB’s count lands a day after the Federal Reserve’s. In its own November Financial Stability Report, the Fed counted more than $3 trillion in signed leases that haven’t started yet, take-or-pay contracts and residual value guarantees at seven big tech companies, none of it showing up as debt, as Fortune reported . The two tallies cover different companies and use different methods.

The ECB’s comparison comes with specifics. In a box on the debt financing of AI , six ECB authors list what looks like 2008: obligations that work like debt but aren’t booked as debt, revenue that loops back to whoever paid for it, credit ratings the bond market may not believe, loans that outlast what they paid for, and leverage building outside the banks. The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission concluded that “a combination of excessive borrowing,…
items.t: European Central Bank sees ‘historical parallels with the dotcom and subprime bubbles’ because of AI’s ‘rapid shift’ into debt finance

items.title: Mississippi gov. says AI infrastructure messaging went sour when it stopped being about necessity: ‘Everybody in America uses data centers regularly’
items.summary:
U.S. voters made their opinions on data centers known at the ballot box this month—opposing data center expansion in 52 of 53 measures in the midterm elections—but Republican Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves believes Americans have lost track of the necessity of the AI infrastructure buildout.

Speaking with Fortune Executive Editor Lee Clifford at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Tuesday, Reeves argued many Americans don’t realize how often they rely on AI infrastructure in their day-to-day lives. He said when he meets with large groups in his state and across the U.S., he tells them to pick up and look at their cell phone, asking if they’ve used the device today, particularly their GPS.

“And if the answer is yes, then you have used a data center today, and everybody in America uses data centers regularly,” Reeves said. “And so, in terms of necessity and the need for everyday American citizens, it is without question that there is going to be a need to keep this data.” 

Mississippi has 38 data center projects total , including 17 operational data centers. Earlier this year, Amazon announced a $25 billion investment in data centers in the state. However, research has overwhelmingly shown Americans oppose local data center construction on the grounds of environmental concerns, as well as fears of climbing utilities bills and electricity costs. 

Reeves argued data centers’ utility goes beyond technology in his constituents’ pockets, and that they are an asset to national security. He cited litigation between the NAACP and xAI, in which the NAACP Mississippi…
items.t: Mississippi gov. says AI infrastructure messaging went sour when it stopped being about necessity: ‘Everybody in America uses data centers regularly’

items.title: ‘This, I’m sorry to say, is just the opening chapter’: Top cyber expert warns of a ‘vulnpocalypse’ after 4 major U.S. systems broke in 6 days
items.summary:
In six days, Microsoft 365 went down, the FAA grounded every flight in the country, customers at Chase and Wells Fargo couldn’t get to their money, and the National Security Agency’s classified internal network went dark. On Tuesday, Nicole Perlroth, one of the best-known voices in cybersecurity, said she was answering hundreds of texts and DMs asking whether the world was ending.

Her answer, in a long post on X : “We are entering a period of unprecedented technological instability.” She called it the “vulnpocalypse.” She also said what she’s hearing doesn’t contradict the official line that most of the breakage comes from “screwy updates.”

That hedge carries the thread, and it matters for every company with a software stack. Microsoft said its nearly 24-hour outage was traced to a bug that came in with a July update to its networking gateway servers, BleepingComputer reported . The FAA’s ground stop ran more than four hours, the longest nationwide halt since the Sept. 11, 2001 shutdown, and more than 9,100 flights were canceled that Friday, according to FlightAware data cited by Fox Weather . Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed “routine maintenance” by a contractor swapping copper wiring for fiber. Chase cited a “technical issue.” Apple said a faulty internal update knocked out iCloud and other customer services on Tuesday. The NSA said its network suffered a “temporary degradation” during routine maintenance. No company or agency has called any of it an attack. Most of it happened while someone was changing or fixing something.

The government’s response came…
items.t: ‘This, I’m sorry to say, is just the opening chapter’: Top cyber expert warns of a ‘vulnpocalypse’ after 4 major U.S. systems broke in 6 days

items.title: Jensen Huang and Nvidia is not a honeypot story. It is a national security story
items.summary:
The consensus view: a brilliant engineer, seduced by a foreign agent. It is also Jensen Huang’s most convenient defense, turning a compliance failure into a private indiscretion. The narrative has one fatal flaw: Mr. Huang himself.

A year ago, we brought the story to The Times of London , worked with the reporter based on our knowledge of the tactics, prompting the article, Beijing’s “sex warfare” in Silicon Valley in which we were quoted, and which Elon Musk summarized: “If she’s a 10, you’re an asset.” This is not a honeypot story, but it may be one of complicity.

Megaspeed, a Singapore company, imported at least 136,000 Nvidia processors worth at least $4.6 billion, Bloomberg reports, more than half were Blackwell chips, restricted from sale to China. It bought through Aivres Systems, the California arm of Inspur, blacklisted for aiding China’s military. A Shanghai sister network, Century Litong facilitated up to $7.5 billion, The Information reports.

The executive at the center of both, Alice Huang, is suspected of spying for China. Officials say he may not have known her role; I make no claim that Mr. Huang did. The affair is not the issue. The transactions are.

The Personal Tenacity 

Mr. Huang rescued Nvidia from near-insolvency, operating “as if it were 30 days from going out of business.” He managed up to 60 direct reports, never grooming a successor and intended to lead for decades. A honeypot trap is designed for the ordinary man, exploiting predictable emotional weaknesses. There is nothing average about Mr. Huang. He is one of a small circle of people that…
items.t: Jensen Huang and Nvidia is not a honeypot story. It is a national security story

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...
items.t: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes

The three-day, invite-only event called Authentic House will fill the hotel’s 170 guest rooms and more than 20 programming spaces with executive meetings, conversations with chief marketing officers about Super Bowl ads, and a presentation of Authentic’s brands and upcoming projects. 

“For us, Super Bowl is more than just a game. It’s like a business summit and a hospitality experience,” Corey Salter , CEO of entertainment at Authentic, told Fortune . “We’re just really trying to create our own headquarters for the biggest weekend in sports.”

Authentic House was created by Authentic Live , the company’s experiences division, which is also behind Shaq’s Fun House and SI: The Party . Authentic Live hosted more than 50 events in 2025, drawing about 65,000 attendees, 324 million social impressions, and more than 35 billion media impressions.

In 2026, the division hosted 58 entertainment events with about 70,000 attendees, generating 643.3 million impressions and 64.4 billion media impressions, which the company attributed partly to the success of O’Neal’s Dunkman . Authentic Live plans to host more than 90 events in 2027. The…

items.title: ‘The Romans are laughing at us’: physical AI founder raises $97 million in quest to stop wasting time with archaic infrastructure maintenance
items.summary:
Alex Hawkinson keeps a collection of Roman artifacts at BrightAI’s robot demo center, and he has a saying to go with them: “The Romans are laughing at us.”

Think of the way the Romans inspected their roads, Hawkinson told Fortune : “They sent teams of technicians out periodically on schedule” to check on their infrastructure. Two thousand years later, power companies, water utilities, and pipeline operators still do. In his telling, two out of three of those trips turn up nothing to fix, and the failures that matter happen in between visits anyway.

Hawkinson is convinced this can change, and investors are paying for the idea. BrightAI said Wednesday it has raised $97 million in a round led by Smith Point Capital , the growth-stage firm started by former Salesforce co-CEO Keith Block. GE Vernova, already a BrightAI customer, also invested, along with Cobalt Capital, Marlinspike Partners, Zero Infinity Partners as well as existing backers Khosla Ventures, Inspired Capital, and Upfront Ventures. The round brings total funding to $184 million and values BrightAI at $750 million, according to a person familiar with the matter. Hawkinson insisted he “doesn’t care” about so-called unicorn status: The point is bring infrastructure out of the ancient Roman era.

His pitch has three parts. Replace scheduled human inspections with sensors and AI that watch infrastructure all the time. Go after what BrightAI estimates is more than $7 trillion a year in waste worldwide. And along the way, create a kind of data that has never existed: a continuous record of how pipes, poles, and pumps…
items.t: ‘The Romans are laughing at us’: physical AI founder raises $97 million in quest to stop wasting time with archaic infrastructure maintenance

items.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
items.summary:
After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

items.title: Robot cage fights and snorting nanoparticles: Notes from the ‘reality distortion field’ of Silicon Valley’s AI frontier
items.summary:
An old mattress showroom on San Francisco’s Van Ness Avenue has recently taken on a new life. Instead of rows of springy California kings, queens, and twin XLs, the space now hosts six-foot-tall humanoid robots—some armed with steel claws—who square off in a small arena to thrash each other with clangy superhuman force. These metal-on-metal cage fights, put on by REK (Robot Entertainment Kombat), inspire a passionate fan base.

Things are moving fast in America’s tech capital. For now, only the mattresses have been displaced. But in a city intent upon reengineering everything from work to the human brain, perhaps one day sleep itself will become outmoded. As we adapt to always-on AI agents and cerebral chip implants, it’s getting harder to know which parts of this imagined future to laugh at, and which to prep for.

Even the workers at AI companies can’t keep up with the blizzard of competing model versions being launched every day. Startups are mixing hardware, software, and biotech, blurring the line between science fiction and the next funding round.

I recently visited a startup in Palo Alto called Subsense that’s developing a brain-computer interface, NanoBCI. The field has been heating up ever since Elon Musk’s Neuralink proved that a wireless computer chip placed on the brain can turn a person’s thoughts into actions .

But while having telekinetic powers would undoubtedly be cool, most people don’t want holes drilled in their skulls. That squeamishness is what Silicon Valley techies call a “barrier to adoption.” And it’s why Subsense is developing a different…
items.t: Robot cage fights and snorting nanoparticles: Notes from the ‘reality distortion field’ of Silicon Valley’s AI frontier

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
items.summary:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: $970 million Pacsun CEO says Gen Alpha and Gen Z are ‘greatly misunderstood’—so she made a board of 12- to 22-year-olds to give her advice
items.summary:
Bosses and senior staffers often moan about how young professionals are disengaged and lack initiative . But Brieane Olson, the CEO of Pacsun, warns against overlooking Gen Z and Gen Alpha—and she’s even ensuring they get a seat at the table of the fashion giant that hit $970 million in sales last year. 

“I definitely felt, having spent so much time on the front line with young consumers, that Gen Z and Gen Alpha were greatly misunderstood,” Olson tells Fortune. “And so, what could we do as a brand that caters to young people to really give them a seat at the table and to build something meaningful and really put community first?”

Every quarter, Pacsun’s Youth Advisory Council gathers with company executives to discuss big business concerns. 

The mini board of directors—comprised of 15 Gen Alpha and Gen Zers aged 12 to 22 who are rotated in each year—weigh in on pressing industry needs, what Pacsun should do differently, and the best paths moving forward. 

The country’s youngest minds bring critical feedback directly to Olson and other company executives, touching upon everything from the customer experience to the way stores operate. 

“I think one of the things that has taught me personally about working with this council over the last two years, is really that working with these younger generations requires sometimes giving additional context. And so it’s really important to bring them along for the journey and to answer the whys before they become a why,” the CEO says. “The most important thing is to truly listen—allow to have a dialogue, be a part of the…
items.t: $970 million Pacsun CEO says Gen Alpha and Gen Z are ‘greatly misunderstood’—so she made a board of 12- to 22-year-olds to give her advice
